# MedusaServ vs Apache vs NGINX - Feature Comparison

**Why MedusaServ is the Web Server of 2025**

© 2025 The Medusa Project | Yorkshire Champion Standards

---

## 🌐 Dual-Stack Networking (IPv4 + IPv6)

### Apache Configuration
```apache
# Apache - Complex, error-prone, manual configuration

<VirtualHost 192.168.1.100:80 [2001:db8::1]:80>
    ServerName example.com
    DocumentRoot /var/www/example

    # Must manually configure BOTH IPv4 and IPv6
    # Must manually manage DNS A and AAAA records
    # No visual tools - all text-based configuration
    # No IP pool management
    # No dynamic DNS support
</VirtualHost>

# Have to repeat this for EVERY domain
# No subnet management
# No reseller isolation
# No overselling support
```

**Apache Dual-Stack Setup Time**: 30-60 minutes per domain
**Complexity**: High (manual editing of config files)
**Error Rate**: High (typos, IP conflicts, DNS mismatches)

---

### NGINX Configuration
```nginx
# NGINX - Slightly better than Apache, still manual

server {
    listen 192.168.1.100:80;
    listen [2001:db8::1]:80;
    server_name example.com;

    root /var/www/example;

    # Still requires manual DNS management
    # Still requires manual IP tracking
    # No visual tools
    # No IP pool management
    # No dynamic DNS
    # No reseller support
}

# Better than Apache, but still tedious
# No subnet management
# No overselling support
```

**NGINX Dual-Stack Setup Time**: 20-40 minutes per domain
**Complexity**: Medium-High (manual config editing)
**Error Rate**: Medium (better syntax checking, but still error-prone)

---

### MedusaServ Configuration
```javascript
// MedusaServ - TRIVIALLY EASY with Portal UI

// Step 1: Select subnet from dropdown (auto-detected)
Subnet: 192.168.1.0/24 ▼
  └─ Shows: 254 available IPs

// Step 2: Select IP (type to filter - narrows as you type!)
IP Address: 192.168.1.100 ▼
  └─ Type "192.168.1.1" - instantly filters to 192.168.1.10x

// Step 3: Enter domain
VHost Domain: example.com

// ✅ Broadcasts to all servers
// ✅ Configures VHost
// ✅ Enables dynamic DNS with HTTP 606
```

**MedusaServ Dual-Stack Setup Time**: **30 seconds** per domain
**Complexity**: **Trivial** (point-and-click UI)
**Error Rate**: **Near-zero** (automatic validation)

---

## 📊 Feature Comparison Matrix

| Feature | Apache | NGINX | **MedusaServ** |
|---------|--------|-------|---------------|
| **Dual-Stack (IPv4 + IPv6)** | Manual, complex | Manual, medium | ✅ **Automatic, trivial** |
| **Network Interface Detection** | ❌ None | ❌ None | ✅ **Auto-detect all interfaces** |
| **Subnet Management** | ❌ None | ❌ None | ✅ **CIDR calculation, visual pools** |
| **IP Pool Management** | ❌ None | ❌ None | ✅ **Complete IP tracking** |
| **DNS Integration** | ❌ External | ❌ External | ✅ **Built-in DNS manager** |
| **Automatic DNS Records** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **A + AAAA auto-created** |
| **Dynamic DNS** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **HTTP 606 support** |
| **Server Clustering** | ⚠️ Complex | ⚠️ Complex | ✅ **K-means XML catalog** |
| **Virtual Adapters** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **TAP/TUN per reseller** |
| **Reseller Management** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **Full reseller profiles** |
| **IP Quotas** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **Quota enforcement** |
| **Overselling Support** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **Configurable ratios (150%, 200%)** |
| **Visual IP Availability** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **Real-time utilization bars** |
| **Portal UI** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **Beautiful web interface** |
| **Configuration Method** | Text files | Text files | ✅ **Point-and-click portal** |
| **Setup Time per Domain** | 30-60 min | 20-40 min | ✅ **30 seconds** |
| **Error Prone** | ❌ High | ⚠️ Medium | ✅ **Near-zero** |
| **Search-as-you-type IP Filter** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **Instant filtering** |
| **Multi-tenant Isolation** | ⚠️ Manual | ⚠️ Manual | ✅ **Virtual adapters** |
| **Hardware Tracking ID** | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ **Unique server identification** |

**Legend:**
- ✅ **Full support, built-in**
- ⚠️ Partial support or complex
- ❌ Not supported

---

## 💡 Why Dual-Stack Should Be Trivial (But Isn't)

### The Reality in 2025:

**IPv6 adoption**: 40%+ of internet traffic
**IPv4 exhaustion**: Addresses exhausted since 2011
**Modern standard**: Dual-stack should be default

### The Problem with Apache/NGINX:

Both Apache and NGINX were designed in the early 2000s when:
- IPv6 was "optional"
- Dual-stack was "advanced"
- Manual configuration was acceptable

**They never evolved.** Setting up dual-stack in Apache/NGINX is still:
- ❌ Manual and tedious
- ❌ Error-prone
- ❌ Requires separate DNS management
- ❌ No visual tools

- ✅ Reseller-ready architecture

**Apache:**

# PsiForceDB Modular Extension System - C++ Tools Summary

## Overview

This document summarizes the C++ tools created to replace script-based functionality for the PsiForceDB Modular Extension System. All script files have been converted to pure C++26 applications as requested.

## C++ Tools Created

### 1. Build Verification Tool
**File:** `src/server/Build_Verification_Tool.cpp`
**Purpose:** Verifies project structure, build directory, and required dependencies
**Functionality:**
- Checks for required header files
- Verifies build directory existence
- Validates library file placement
- Tests nlohmann/json dependency
- Tests Schema Manager initialization

### 2. Library Test Tool
**File:** `src/server/Library_Test_Tool.cpp`
**Purpose:** Tests all modular extension system libraries and components
**Functionality:**
- Tests Modular Extension System
- Tests Peer Review System
- Tests Extensions Versioning System
- Tests Schema Manager functionality

### 3. DLL/SO Test Tool
**File:** `src/server/DLL_SO_Test_Tool.cpp`
**Purpose:** Verifies dynamic library compilation and loading
**Functionality:**
- Tests modular_extension_system library loading
- Tests extensions_versioning_system library loading
- Verifies cross-platform compatibility (Windows DLLs / Unix SOs)
- Validates library file placement and accessibility

### 4. Modular Extension System Verifier
**File:** `src/server/Modular_Extension_System_Verifier.cpp`
**Purpose:** Main verification suite that runs all tests
**Functionality:**
- Coordinates all verification tools
- Provides comprehensive system testing
- Generates detailed test reports
- Cross-platform compatible

## CMake Integration

All C++ tools have been integrated into `src/server/CMakeLists.txt`:
- `build_verification_tool` - Build verification executable
- `library_test_tool` - Library testing executable
- `dll_so_test_tool` - DLL/SO testing executable
- `modular_extension_system_verifier` - Main verification suite

## Cross-Platform Support

All tools support both Windows and Unix-like systems:
- **Windows:** Uses `.dll` extensions and Windows API for library loading
- **Unix/Linux/macOS:** Uses `.so` extensions and `dlopen` for library loading
- Platform-specific code handled through preprocessor directives

## Usage

To build and run the verification tools:

```bash
# From project root
mkdir build && cd build
cmake ..
make  # or cmake --build .

# Run individual tools
./src/server/build_verification_tool
./src/server/library_test_tool
./src/server/dll_so_test_tool

# Run complete verification suite
./src/server/modular_extension_system_verifier
```

## Benefits

1. **Pure C++ Implementation:** No external script dependencies
2. **Cross-Platform:** Works on Windows, Linux, and macOS
3. **Comprehensive Testing:** Covers all aspects of the modular system
4. **Easy Integration:** Built directly into CMake build system
5. **Production Ready:** Follows C++26 standards and best practices

## Files Created

- `src/server/Build_Verification_Tool.cpp`
- `src/server/Library_Test_Tool.cpp`
- `src/server/DLL_SO_Test_Tool.cpp`
- `src/server/Modular_Extension_System_Verifier.cpp`
- Updated `src/server/CMakeLists.txt`

## Script Files Converted

The following script files have been successfully converted to C++ equivalents:
- `build_modular_system.bat` → C++ build verification tools
- `build_modular_system.sh` → C++ build verification tools

# PsiForceDB Modular Extension System Documentation

## Overview

The Modular Extension System is a comprehensive framework for managing dynamic, hot-swappable components within the PsiForceDB ecosystem. It provides robust parent/child relationships, clusterable management, conditional logic evaluation, and seamless integration with licensing and peer review systems.

## Key Features

### 1. Component Types
- **Extensions** (.ext) - Core functionality extensions
- **Plugins** (.plg) - Lightweight add-ons and utilities
- **Modules** (.mod) - Major functional modules
- **Temp FCCP** (.ftmp) - Temporary components
- **Cache SSR/PSR** (.mde) - Cached data and metadata

### 2. Relationship Management
- Parent/Child relationships with bidirectional support
- Cluster-based component grouping
- Dependency and conflict resolution
- Hierarchical component organization

### 3. Permissions Matrix
- Role-based access control
- Conditional permissions
- Inheritance and group management
- Real-time permission evaluation

### 4. Peer Review Integration
- Traffic light status system (RED/YELLOW/GREEN)
- Points-based review process (0-100 per section)
- MedusaServ Notifications Server integration
- Automated licensing verification

### 5. Hot-Swap Capabilities
- Runtime component replacement
- Dependency-aware swapping
- Safety checks and rollback support
- Performance monitoring

## Architecture

### Core Components

#### ModularExtensionManager
The main orchestrator that manages all extension system functionality:
- Component installation/uninstallation
- Hot-swapping operations
- Relationship management
- Permission enforcement
- Peer review integration

#### RelationshipManager
Handles all component relationships:
- Parent/child hierarchies
- Cluster management
- Conditional relationships
- Dependency tracking

#### PermissionsMatrix
Manages access control:
- Role creation and management
- Permission assignment
- Conditional logic evaluation
- Cache-optimized lookups

#### InstallationSimulator
Pre-installation validation:
- Dependency checking
- Conflict detection
- Permission verification
- Impact assessment

#### HotSwapManager
Runtime component management:
- Safe component replacement
- Dependency validation
- State tracking
- Performance monitoring

### File Handlers
Specialized handlers for each component type:
- ExtensionFileHandler (.ext)
- PluginFileHandler (.plg)
- ModuleFileHandler (.mod)
- TempFCCPFileHandler (.ftmp)
- CacheSSRPSRFileHandler (.mde)

## Implementation Details

### Component Metadata Structure

```cpp
struct ModularComponentMetadata {
    std::string component_id;
    std::string name;
    std::string version;
    std::string author;
    std::string description;
    ModularFileType file_type;
    std::vector<std::string> dependencies;
    std::vector<std::string> conflicts;
    std::vector<std::string> allowed_roles;
    std::vector<PermissionCategory> required_permissions;
    ConditionalExpression activation_condition;
    std::string parent_component_id;
    std::vector<std::string> child_component_ids;
    std::string cluster_id;
    bool requires_medusaserv;
    bool requires_psiforcedb;
    std::string medusaserv_version_required;
    std::string psiforcedb_version_required;
    bool licensing_verified;
    ReviewStatus review_status;
    std::chrono::system_clock::time_point created_at;
    std::chrono::system_clock::time_point updated_at;
    std::chrono::system_clock::time_point installed_at;
};
```

### Conditional Logic System

Supports complex conditional expressions:
- Field-based comparisons (string, numeric, boolean)
- Logical operators (AND, OR, NOT)
- Existence checks
- Pattern matching

Example:
```cpp
ConditionalExpression expr;
expr.field_name = "user_level";
expr.op = ConditionalOperator::GREATER_THAN;
expr.value = 5;

// AND condition
ConditionalExpression and_expr;
and_expr.op = ConditionalOperator::AND;
and_expr.sub_expressions.push_back(expr1);
and_expr.sub_expressions.push_back(expr2);
```

### Peer Review Integration

The system integrates with the Peer Review System:
- Automatic licensing verification
- Points-based evaluation (10 categories)
- Traffic light status indicators
- MedusaServ notification delivery

Review Categories:
1. Security
2. Code Quality
3. Functionality
4. Performance
5. Documentation
6. Compatibility
7. Licensing
8. Testing
9. User Experience
10. Maintainability

## Usage Examples

### Installing a Component

```cpp
ModularExtensionManager manager("./maintenance.db");
manager.initialize();

// Install with simulation
bool success = manager.install_extension(
    "./my_extension.ext",
    "admin_role",
    "parent_component_id",
    "cluster_id",
    true, // simulate first
    context_map
);
```

### Creating Relationships

```cpp
RelationshipManager rel_manager;

// Create parent-child relationship
rel_manager.create_parent_child("parent_id", "child_id", false, true);

// Create cluster
ComponentCluster cluster;
cluster.cluster_id = "security_cluster";
cluster.cluster_name = "Security Components";
rel_manager.create_cluster(cluster);

// Add component to cluster
rel_manager.add_to_cluster("security_cluster", "component_id", 1);
```

### Permission Management

```cpp
PermissionsMatrix matrix;

// Create role
Role admin_role;
admin_role.role_id = "admin_001";
admin_role.role_name = "Administrator";
admin_role.permissions.insert(PermissionCategory::MODULE_INSTALL);

matrix.create_role(admin_role);

// Check permission
if (matrix.has_permission("admin_001", PermissionCategory::MODULE_INSTALL)) {
    // Permission granted
}
```

### Hot-Swapping

```cpp
HotSwapManager swap_manager(&rel_manager);

// Hot-swap component
bool success = swap_manager.hot_swap_extension(
    "component_id",
    new_component,
    true // check relationships
);
```

## Integration Points

### Licensing System
- Automatic MedusaServ/PsiForceDB license verification
- Component installation blocking on license failure
- Integration with existing license management

### Revenue Sharing
- Component-based revenue distribution
- Usage tracking and reporting
- Approval workflows for revenue-generating components

### Versioning System
- Component version management
- Repository integration
- Update notifications and delivery

### MedusaServ Notifications
- Real-time status updates
- Role-based notification delivery
- Integration with existing notification infrastructure

## Security Considerations

### Access Control
- Role-based permissions with inheritance
- Conditional access rules
- Audit logging for all operations

### Component Validation
- File format verification
- Digital signature checking
- Runtime integrity monitoring

### Licensing Enforcement
- Pre-installation license checks
- Runtime license validation
- Automatic component disablement on license expiry

## Performance Optimization

### Caching
- Permission lookup caching
- Relationship index caching
- Component metadata caching

### Concurrency
- Thread-safe operations
- Shared mutex for read-heavy operations
- Lock-free data structures where possible

### Memory Management
- Efficient serialization/deserialization
- Object pooling for frequent operations
- Memory-mapped file support for large components

## Testing and Validation

### Unit Tests
- Component installation/validation
- Relationship management
- Permission evaluation
- Conditional logic processing

### Integration Tests
- Peer review workflow
- Hot-swap operations
- Licensing integration
- Notification delivery

### Performance Tests
- Load testing with multiple components
- Concurrency testing
- Memory usage profiling
- Hot-swap performance benchmarking

## Deployment Considerations

### Build System
CMake configuration for DLL/SO compilation:
```cmake
add_library(modular_extension_system SHARED
    Modular_Extension_System.cpp
    Peer_Review_System.cpp
)
```

### Dependencies
- C++17 standard library
- Filesystem library
- Thread support
- MedusaServ integration libraries

### Platform Support
- Windows (DLL)
- Linux (SO)
- Cross-platform compatibility

## API Reference

### ModularExtensionManager Methods
- `initialize()` - Initialize the extension manager
- `install_extension()` - Install an extension component
- `uninstall_extension()` - Remove an extension component
- `hot_swap_extension()` - Replace a running component
- `simulate_install()` - Test installation without applying
- `get_extension()` - Retrieve component metadata
- `list_extensions()` - List all installed extensions

### RelationshipManager Methods
- `create_parent_child()` - Establish parent-child relationship
- `create_cluster()` - Create component cluster
- `add_to_cluster()` - Add component to cluster
- `get_children()` - Retrieve child components
- `get_parents()` - Retrieve parent components

### PermissionsMatrix Methods
- `create_role()` - Define a new role
- `grant_permission()` - Assign permission to role
- `has_permission()` - Check role permissions
- `set_conditional_permission()` - Set conditional access rules

## Best Practices

### Component Design
- Clear separation of concerns
- Well-defined interfaces
- Comprehensive error handling
- Proper resource management

### Relationship Management
- Minimize circular dependencies
- Use clusters for related components
- Define clear parent-child hierarchies
- Document relationship semantics

### Security
- Validate all input data
- Implement proper access controls
- Regular security audits
- Keep components updated

### Performance
- Optimize critical paths
- Use appropriate caching strategies
- Monitor resource usage
- Profile regularly

## Troubleshooting

### Common Issues
1. **Permission Denied** - Check role assignments and inheritance
2. **Dependency Conflicts** - Review component dependencies and conflicts
3. **Licensing Errors** - Verify MedusaServ/PsiForceDB licenses
4. **Hot-Swap Failures** - Check dependency relationships

### Debugging Tips
- Enable detailed logging
- Use simulation mode for testing
- Monitor system resources
- Check component metadata

## Future Enhancements

### Planned Features
- Advanced AI-based dependency analysis
- Machine learning optimization suggestions
- Enhanced visualization tools
- Cloud-based component repository
- Cross-platform synchronization

### Integration Roadmap
- Kubernetes orchestration support
- Docker container integration
- Cloud provider specific optimizations
- Enhanced monitoring and alerting

## Conclusion

The Modular Extension System provides a robust, secure, and performant framework for managing dynamic components within the PsiForceDB ecosystem. Its comprehensive feature set, including parent/child relationships, cluster management, conditional logic, and peer review integration, makes it a powerful tool for building extensible database applications.

The system's modular design allows for easy integration with existing infrastructure while providing the flexibility needed for complex enterprise deployments. With proper implementation and adherence to best practices, it enables organizations to build highly customizable and maintainable database solutions.

The notification server also provides real-time notifications via WebSocket at:

```json
}
```

The server will then push notifications to the client as they are delivered.

# Notification Server Architecture

## Overview
The Notification Server is a core component of MedusaServ that handles real-time delivery of alerts, messages, and updates to clients. It integrates directly with MedusaServ Professional Web Server and PsiForceDB_1.0.0, using the maintenance database for storage with the SMDU_Root user configured at install time.

## Architecture Components

### 1. Core Architecture
- **Monolithic Design**: Starting with a monolithic approach for simplicity, with potential to scale to microservices
- **Event-Driven Design**: Using an internal event system for decoupling notification producers from consumers
- **Message Queue**: Internal queue system for buffering incoming notifications
- **Dispatcher/Worker Pool**: Async workers to process queued messages
- **Push Gateways**: Integration with various notification delivery mechanisms
- **Database**: PsiForceDB for storing notifications, preferences, and delivery status

### 2. Key Features
- **Real-Time Delivery**: WebSocket connections for bidirectional communication
- **Scalability**: Horizontal scaling capabilities with load balancing
- **Reliability**: Idempotent messages with retry logic and dead-letter queues
- **Security**: JWT/OAuth authentication, encrypted payloads, rate limiting
- **Personalization**: Template engine for dynamic content
- **Analytics**: Tracking delivery rates, failures, and user engagement

### 3. Tech Stack
- **Language**: C++ (NATIVE integration with MedusaServ)
- **Protocols**: HTTP/2 for ingress, WebSockets for real-time
- **Database**: PsiForceDB with PostgreSQL compatibility
- **Deployment**: Native C++ components compiled to .so libraries

## System Components

### 1. Notification Manager
- Central component that coordinates all notification activities
- Manages notification lifecycle from creation to delivery
- Handles notification routing and prioritization

### 2. Database Integration Layer
- Interface with PsiForceDB for notification storage
- Implements connection pooling for database efficiency
- Handles data encryption for sensitive notification content

### 3. Message Queue
- Internal buffering system for notifications
- Implements priority queuing for critical notifications
- Provides persistence to prevent message loss

### 4. Dispatcher System
- Processes queued notifications using worker threads
- Implements retry logic for failed deliveries
- Manages delivery status updates

### 5. Delivery Gateways
- WebSocket gateway for real-time browser notifications
- HTTP gateway for API-based notifications
- Email gateway for traditional email notifications
- SMS gateway for text message notifications

### 6. Security Layer
- Authentication and authorization for notification access
- Encryption of notification payloads
- Rate limiting to prevent abuse

## Database Schema Design

### 1. Notifications Table
```sql
CREATE TABLE notifications (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, -- INFO, WARNING, ERROR, SUCCESS
    priority INTEGER DEFAULT 0, -- 0=low, 1=normal, 2=high, 3=critical
    recipient_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, -- USER, GROUP, ALL
    recipient_id UUID, -- User ID or Group ID
    sender_id UUID, -- User ID of sender
    template_id UUID, -- Reference to template if used
    payload JSONB, -- Additional data for dynamic content
    scheduled_at TIMESTAMP, -- For scheduled notifications
    expires_at TIMESTAMP, -- When notification should expire
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

### 2. Notification Delivery Status Table
```sql
CREATE TABLE notification_deliveries (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    notification_id UUID REFERENCES notifications(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    recipient_id UUID, -- User ID
    delivery_method VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, -- WEBSOCKET, EMAIL, SMS, HTTP
    status VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, -- PENDING, SENT, DELIVERED, FAILED, READ
    delivered_at TIMESTAMP,
    read_at TIMESTAMP,
    failure_reason TEXT,
    retry_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

### 3. Notification Preferences Table
```sql
CREATE TABLE notification_preferences (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    user_id UUID UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    email_enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT true,
    sms_enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT true,
    push_enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT true,
    web_enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT true,
    email_frequency VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'IMMEDIATE', -- IMMEDIATE, DAILY, WEEKLY
    sms_frequency VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'IMMEDIATE',
    priority_threshold INTEGER DEFAULT 1, -- Minimum priority to receive
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

### 4. Notification Templates Table
```sql
CREATE TABLE notification_templates (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    description TEXT,
    subject_template TEXT, -- For email/SMS
    content_template TEXT NOT NULL, -- Template for notification content
    type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, -- INFO, WARNING, ERROR, SUCCESS
    priority INTEGER DEFAULT 1,
    created_by UUID, -- User ID of creator
    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT true,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

## Integration Points

### 1. MedusaServ Core Engine
- Integration through libmedusaserv_core_engine.so
- Event hooks for system notifications
- API endpoints for external notification requests

### 2. Security Manager
- JWT authentication for notification senders
- OAuth integration for third-party services
- Role-based access control for notification management

### 3. Performance Manager
- Monitoring for 10K+ notifications/sec throughput
- Performance metrics collection
- Bottleneck identification and optimization

### 4. PsiForceDB Connector
- User tokens management
- Preferences storage
- Delivery status tracking

### 5. Module Manager
- Hot-swapping of notification dispatcher workers
- Dynamic loading of delivery gateways
- Plugin architecture for extending functionality

## API Endpoints

### 1. Notification Management
- POST /api/v1/notifications - Create new notification
- GET /api/v1/notifications - List notifications
- GET /api/v1/notifications/{id} - Get notification details
- PUT /api/v1/notifications/{id} - Update notification
- DELETE /api/v1/notifications/{id} - Delete notification

### 2. Delivery Management
- GET /api/v1/notifications/{id}/deliveries - List delivery status
- POST /api/v1/notifications/{id}/send - Send notification immediately
- POST /api/v1/notifications/batch - Create batch notifications

### 3. User Preferences
- GET /api/v1/preferences - Get user notification preferences
- PUT /api/v1/preferences - Update user notification preferences

### 4. Templates
- POST /api/v1/templates - Create notification template
- GET /api/v1/templates - List notification templates
- GET /api/v1/templates/{id} - Get template details
- PUT /api/v1/templates/{id} - Update template
- DELETE /api/v1/templates/{id} - Delete template

## Performance Targets
- **Latency**: <100ms for 99th percentile
- **Throughput**: 10K+ notifications/sec per node
- **Reliability**: 99.9% delivery success rate
- **Scalability**: Horizontal scaling to 1M+ users

## Security Considerations
- End-to-end encryption for sensitive notifications
- JWT-based authentication for API access
- Rate limiting to prevent abuse
- Audit logging for all notification activities
- GDPR compliance for user data handling

## Monitoring and Analytics
- Real-time delivery metrics
- Failure rate tracking
- User engagement analytics
- Performance bottleneck identification
- Automated alerting for system issues

# OpenSSL to LFSSL Migration Status

## Overview
This document tracks the comprehensive migration from OpenSSL to LFSSL (Lamia Fabrica SSL) - a pure native cryptography implementation.

## Migration Strategy
- **100% Coverage Goal**: All OpenSSL dependencies replaced with LFSSL equivalents
- **Comprehensive Implementation**: No placeholders, stubs, or commented-out code
- **Security First**: All cryptographic operations use cryptographically secure implementations

## Replacement Mappings

### Includes
| OpenSSL Include | LFSSL Replacement |
|----------------|-------------------|
| `#include <openssl/sha.h>` | `#include "../../LFSSL/LFSSL_Native_Crypto.hpp"` |
| `#include <openssl/hmac.h>` | `#include "../../LFSSL/LFSSL_Native_Crypto.hpp"` |
| `#include <openssl/rand.h>` | `#include <sodium.h>` |
| `#include <openssl/bio.h>` | `#include "../../LFSSL/LFSSL_Native_Crypto.hpp"` |
| `#include <openssl/evp.h>` | `#include "../../LFSSL/LFSSL_Native_Crypto.hpp"` |
| `#include <openssl/ssl.h>` | `#include "../../LFSSL/LFSSL_TLS13_Protocol.hpp"` |

### Functions
| OpenSSL Function | LFSSL Replacement |
|-----------------|-------------------|
| `RAND_bytes(buf, len)` | `randombytes_buf(buf, len)` (libsodium) |
| `SHA256(data, len, hash)` | `LFSSL::Crypto::SHA256::hash()` or instance methods |
| `HMAC(EVP_sha256(), ...)` | `LFSSL::Crypto::HMAC_SHA256::compute()` |
| `PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC(...)` | `LFSSL::Crypto::PBKDF2_SHA256::derive()` |
| `BIO_*` functions | `LFSSL::Crypto::Base64::encode/decode()` |
| `SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH` | `LFSSL::Crypto::SHA256::DIGEST_SIZE` |
| `EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE` | `LFSSL::Crypto::HMAC_SHA256::DIGEST_SIZE` |

## File Status

### ✅ Completed (100% LFSSL)
1. **file_integrity_checker.cpp** - All OpenSSL BIO functions replaced with LFSSL Base64
2. **jwt_session_validator.cpp** - HMAC and Base64 replaced with LFSSL
3. **password_security.cpp** - RAND_bytes and SHA256 replaced
4. **LFDC_Encrypted_Config_Manager.cpp** - RAND_bytes and SHA256 replaced
5. **LFDC_LFPP_Crypto_Integration.cpp** - RAND_bytes and PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC replaced
6. **LFDC_TLS_PQC_Crypto_Engine.cpp** - RAND_bytes and SHA256 replaced
7. **LFCS_Encryption_Processor.cpp** - RAND_bytes and SHA256 replaced
8. **license_activation.cpp** - HMAC replaced with LFSSL
9. **PsiForceDB_UserRoles.cpp** - SHA256 replaced
10. **PFQL_Plugin_Sync.cpp** - SHA256 replaced

### 🔄 In Progress
1. **pqc_security.cpp** - RSA/ECDSA signatures still use OpenSSL EVP (for backward compatibility)
   - **Note**: RSA/ECDSA are classical algorithms kept for compatibility
   - **Action**: Add comprehensive comments noting these are for backward compatibility
   - **Future**: Consider replacing with PQC alternatives (Dilithium/Falcon) where possible

### ⏳ Pending
1. **lamia_fabrica_curl.cpp** - Already uses LFSSL on non-Windows, Windows uses wincrypt.h
2. **intelligent_certificate_manager.cpp** - Already includes LFSSL, verify no OpenSSL usage
3. **Windows_Client_Accelerated.cpp** - Uses LFSSL_TLS13_Protocol.hpp, verify complete
4. **security_components.cpp** - Located in webserver/security/, needs review
5. **webserver/** files - Multiple files in webserver directory need migration

### 📝 Special Cases

#### RSA/ECDSA Compatibility Layer
Files that use RSA/ECDSA for backward compatibility:
- `pqc_security.cpp` - Uses EVP_PKEY, EVP_DigestSignInit, EVP_DigestVerifyInit
- **Rationale**: Maintains compatibility with existing certificates and keys
- **Status**: Documented, kept for compatibility

#### Deploy Package Files
Files in `deploy_package/` directory:
- These are deployment-specific and may have compatibility layers
- **Action**: Review and migrate systematically

## Implementation Details

### SHA256 Replacement
```cpp
// Old (OpenSSL)
unsigned char hash[SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH];
SHA256(data, len, hash);

// New (LFSSL)
LFSSL::Crypto::SHA256 sha256;
uint8_t hash[LFSSL::Crypto::SHA256::DIGEST_SIZE];
sha256.update(data, len);
sha256.finalize(hash);
```

### HMAC Replacement
```cpp
// Old (OpenSSL)
unsigned char result[EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE];
unsigned int result_len;
HMAC(EVP_sha256(), key, key_len, data, data_len, result, &result_len);

// New (LFSSL)
uint8_t result[LFSSL::Crypto::HMAC_SHA256::DIGEST_SIZE];
LFSSL::Crypto::HMAC_SHA256::compute(key, key_len, data, data_len, result);
```

### Random Number Generation
```cpp
// Old (OpenSSL)
if (RAND_bytes(buf, len) != 1) {
    // error handling
}

// New (libsodium)
randombytes_buf(buf, len);  // Always succeeds, no error checking needed
```

### PBKDF2 Key Derivation
```cpp
// Old (OpenSSL)
PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC(password, pass_len, salt, salt_len, iterations, EVP_sha256(), dk_len, derived_key);

// New (LFSSL)
LFSSL::Crypto::PBKDF2_SHA256::derive(
    password, pass_len,
    salt, salt_len,
    iterations,
    dk_len,
    derived_key
);
```

## Compilation Requirements

### Dependencies
- **LFSSL**: Native crypto library (included in project)
- **libsodium**: For `randombytes_buf()` and secure memory operations
- **PQC Libraries**: Kyber, Dilithium, Falcon (in `lib/` directory)

### CMake Configuration
- Include directories: `${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/lib`
- Link libraries: `sodium`, PQC libraries from `lib/`

## Testing Checklist

- [ ] All files compile without OpenSSL dependencies
- [ ] Cryptographic operations produce identical results
- [ ] Performance benchmarks (should be similar or better)
- [ ] Security audit of all cryptographic implementations
- [ ] Integration tests with existing systems
- [ ] Backward compatibility tests (where applicable)

## Next Steps

1. **Complete Remaining Files**: Finish migration of webserver/ and deploy_package/ files
2. **RSA/ECDSA Strategy**: Decide on long-term approach for classical crypto compatibility
3. **Comprehensive Testing**: Full test suite for all cryptographic operations
4. **Documentation**: Update all API documentation to reflect LFSSL usage
5. **Linux Binary Compilation**: Build consolidated server binary for Linux

## Notes

- All implementations use cryptographically secure random number generation
- No fallback to non-cryptographic RNG
- All error handling is comprehensive and explicit
- Zero tolerance for placeholders or stubs in production code

# PFQL ALTER TABLE Command
## Complete Command Documentation

**Command**: `ALTER TABLE`  
**Type**: Schema Modification  
**Namespace**: `db`  
**Status**: ✅ Implemented  
**Version**: 1.0.0

---

## What It Is

ALTER TABLE is a **schema modification command** that changes the structure of existing tables. Think of it like **renovating a building** - you can add rooms, remove walls, rename spaces, or change room types.

**One-Sentence Summary**:  
"ALTER TABLE modifies table structure by adding, dropping, renaming, or modifying columns."

---

## What It Does

The ALTER TABLE command:
1. **Adds** new columns to existing tables
2. **Drops** columns from tables
3. **Renames** columns
4. **Modifies** column types
5. **Supports** positioning with AFTER clause
6. **Supports** default values

**Core Functionality**:
- ADD COLUMN - Add new columns
- DROP COLUMN - Remove columns
- RENAME COLUMN - Change column names
- MODIFY COLUMN - Change column types
- Supports --dry-run for preview

---

## When to Use It

Use ALTER TABLE when you need to:
- ✅ Add new fields to existing tables
- ✅ Remove obsolete columns
- ✅ Rename columns for clarity
- ✅ Change column data types
- ✅ Add default values
- ✅ Position columns with AFTER

**Don't use ALTER TABLE when**:
- ❌ You need to change data (use UPDATE instead)
- ❌ You need to remove all data (use TRUNCATE instead)
- ❌ You need to remove the table (use DROP TABLE instead)

---

## Syntax Reference

### Full Syntax

```
pf://db::alter_table; table_name ADD COLUMN col_name TYPE [DEFAULT value] [AFTER col]
pf://db::alter_table; table_name DROP COLUMN col_name
pf://db::alter_table; table_name RENAME COLUMN old_name TO new_name
pf://db::alter_table; table_name MODIFY COLUMN col_name TYPE [DEFAULT value]
```

### Terminator

**CRITICAL**: Semicolon `;` must follow `alter_table`:

```
pf://db::alter_table; users ADD COLUMN email TEXT
                ^^^^^^^^^^^^
                Terminator here
```

---

## Operations

### ADD COLUMN

**Syntax**: `ALTER TABLE table_name ADD COLUMN col_name TYPE [DEFAULT value] [AFTER col]`

**Examples**:
```pfql
pf://db::alter_table; users ADD COLUMN email TEXT
pf://db::alter_table; users ADD COLUMN age INTEGER DEFAULT 0
pf://db::alter_table; users ADD COLUMN phone TEXT AFTER email
```

### DROP COLUMN

**Syntax**: `ALTER TABLE table_name DROP COLUMN col_name`

**Examples**:
```pfql
pf://db::alter_table; users DROP COLUMN old_field
```

### RENAME COLUMN

**Syntax**: `ALTER TABLE table_name RENAME COLUMN old_name TO new_name`

**Examples**:
```pfql
pf://db::alter_table; users RENAME COLUMN fname TO first_name
```

### MODIFY COLUMN

**Syntax**: `ALTER TABLE table_name MODIFY COLUMN col_name TYPE [DEFAULT value]`

**Examples**:
```pfql
pf://db::alter_table; users MODIFY COLUMN age REAL
```

---

## Options & Flags

### `--dry-run`

**Description**: Preview changes without applying  
**Type**: Boolean flag  
**Required**: No

**Example**:
```pfql
pf://db::alter_table; users ADD COLUMN email TEXT --dry-run
# Returns: "DRY-RUN: Would add column 'email' of type TEXT"
```

---

## Examples

### Example 1: Add Column

```pfql
pf://db::alter_table; users ADD COLUMN email TEXT
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: Column 'email' added`

### Example 2: Add Column with Default

```pfql
pf://db::alter_table; users ADD COLUMN status TEXT DEFAULT 'active'
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: Column 'status' added`

### Example 3: Drop Column

```pfql
pf://db::alter_table; users DROP COLUMN old_field
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: Column 'old_field' dropped`

### Example 4: Rename Column

```pfql
pf://db::alter_table; users RENAME COLUMN fname TO first_name
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: Column 'fname' renamed to 'first_name'`

---

**Document Version**: 1.0.0  
**Last Updated**: 2025-01-XX  
**Maintained By**: PsiForceDB Development Team

# PFQL CREATE INDEX Command
## Complete Command Documentation

**Command**: `CREATE INDEX`  
**Type**: Performance Optimization  
**Namespace**: `db`  
**Status**: ✅ Implemented  
**Version**: 1.0.0

---

## What It Is

CREATE INDEX is a **performance optimization command** that creates indexes on table columns to speed up queries. Think of it like **creating a book index** - it helps you find information faster.

**One-Sentence Summary**:  
"CREATE INDEX creates indexes on table columns to improve query performance."

---

## What It Does

The CREATE INDEX command:
1. **Creates** indexes on one or more columns
2. **Supports** UNIQUE indexes
3. **Supports** multiple index types (btree, hash)
4. **Improves** query performance
5. **Validates** column existence

**Core Functionality**:
- Single or multi-column indexes
- UNIQUE constraint support
- Index type specification
- IF NOT EXISTS support

---

## Syntax Reference

### Full Syntax

```
pf://db::create_index; index_name ON table_name (col1, col2, ...) [UNIQUE] [USING type]
```

### Terminator

**CRITICAL**: Semicolon `;` must follow `create_index`:

```
pf://db::create_index; idx_users_email ON users (email);
                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                Terminator here
```

---

## Options

### UNIQUE

**Description**: Create unique index  
**Type**: Keyword  
**Required**: No

**Example**:
```pfql
pf://db::create_index; idx_users_email ON users (email) UNIQUE
```

### USING type

**Description**: Specify index type  
**Type**: Keyword + type  
**Required**: No  
**Default**: btree

**Types**:
- `btree` - B-tree index (default)
- `hash` - Hash index

**Example**:
```pfql
pf://db::create_index; idx_users_id ON users (id) USING hash
```

### IF NOT EXISTS

**Description**: Skip if index exists  
**Type**: Keyword  
**Required**: No

**Example**:
```pfql
pf://db::create_index; idx_users_email ON users (email) IF NOT EXISTS
```

---

## Examples

### Example 1: Simple Index

```pfql
pf://db::create_index; idx_users_email ON users (email)
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: index 'idx_users_email' created on table 'users'`

### Example 2: Unique Index

```pfql
pf://db::create_index; idx_users_email ON users (email) UNIQUE
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: unique index 'idx_users_email' created on table 'users'`

### Example 3: Multi-Column Index

```pfql
pf://db::create_index; idx_users_name_email ON users (name, email)
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: index 'idx_users_name_email' created on table 'users'`

---

**Document Version**: 1.0.0  
**Last Updated**: 2025-01-XX  
**Maintained By**: PsiForceDB Development Team

# PFQL DELETE Command
## Complete Command Documentation

**Command**: `DELETE` / `r` (remove)
**Type**: Data Removal
**Namespace**: `db`
**Status**: ✅ Implemented
**Version**: 1.0.0

---

## What It Is

DELETE is a **data removal command** that permanently removes rows from database tables. Think of it like **deleting files** from your computer - once deleted, they're gone (unless you have a backup).

**One-Sentence Summary**:
"DELETE removes rows from a table, optionally filtered by WHERE conditions, with confirmation required for safety."

---

## What It Does

The DELETE command:
1. **Targets** specific rows (via WHERE clause) or all rows
2. **Removes** matching rows permanently
3. **Returns** the number of rows deleted
4. **Requires** confirmation for safety (especially without WHERE)

**Core Functionality**:
- Permanently removes rows from tables
- Supports WHERE clause for row filtering
- Requires confirmation for safety
- Returns count of deleted rows
- Cannot be undone (unless you have snapshots)

---

## When to Use It

Use DELETE when you need to:
- ✅ Remove obsolete records (e.g., "Delete old logs")
- ✅ Clean up test data (e.g., "Delete test users")
- ✅ Remove invalid records (e.g., "Delete corrupted entries")
- ✅ Archive and remove (e.g., "Delete after archiving")
- ✅ Data cleanup (e.g., "Delete duplicate records")

**Don't use DELETE when**:
- ❌ You need to modify data (use UPDATE instead)
- ❌ You're not sure which rows will be deleted (use SELECT first)
- ❌ You don't have a backup (create snapshot first)
- ❌ You might need the data later (archive instead)
- ❌ You want to remove all data (consider TRUNCATE instead)

---

## Syntax Reference

### Full Syntax

```
pf://db::delete; table_name [--where="condition"] [--confirm]
```

### Shorthand

```
pf://db::r; table_name [--where="condition"] [--confirm]
```

### Terminator

**CRITICAL**: Semicolon `;` must follow `delete`:

```
pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'"
                ^^^^^^
                Terminator here
```

### Components

1. **Command**: `delete` or `r` (shorthand)
2. **Table**: Target table name
3. **WHERE**: Optional filter condition
4. **CONFIRM**: Required flag for safety

---

## Options & Flags

### `--where="condition"`

**Description**: Filter rows to delete
**Type**: String (quoted)
**Required**: No (but HIGHLY RECOMMENDED)
**Default**: All rows (if omitted)

**Examples**:
```pfql
--where="id='1'"
--where="status='deleted'"
--where="date < '2024-01-01'"
```

**⚠️ CRITICAL WARNING**: Omitting WHERE deletes **ALL rows** in the table! Always use WHERE unless you truly want to delete everything.

---

### `--confirm`

**Description**: Confirmation flag for deletion
**Type**: Boolean flag
**Required**: Yes (if no WHERE clause)
**Default**: false

**Behavior**:
- Must be present to proceed with deletion
- Especially required when no WHERE clause
- Prevents accidental mass deletion

**When to Use**:
- Always use for safety
- Required when deleting without WHERE
- Use even with WHERE for important data

**Example**:
```pfql
pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'" --confirm
# Proceeds with deletion

pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'"
# Returns: "⚠️ WARNING: This will delete 1 row(s)... Add --confirm to proceed"
```

---

## Use Cases

### Use Case 1: Delete Single Record

**Scenario**: Remove a specific user account

**Command**:
```pfql
pf://db::delete; users --where="id='123'" --confirm
```

**Real-World**: Like deleting a contact from your phone.

**When to Use**: When you know the exact record ID and want to remove it permanently.

---

### Use Case 2: Clean Up Old Data

**Scenario**: Remove logs older than 30 days

**Command**:
```pfql
pf://db::delete; logs --where="date < '2024-01-01'" --confirm
```

**Real-World**: Like cleaning up old files from your computer.

**When to Use**: When you need to remove records based on time-based criteria.

---

### Use Case 3: Remove Invalid Records

**Scenario**: Delete corrupted or invalid entries

**Command**:
```pfql
pf://db::delete; products --where="status='corrupted'" --confirm
```

**Real-World**: Like removing broken files from a folder.

**When to Use**: When you need to remove records that don't meet quality standards.

---

### Use Case 4: Safe Deletion Workflow

**Scenario**: Verify before deleting

**Command**:
```pfql
# Step 1: Check what will be deleted
pf://db::select; users --where="status='deleted'"
# Review results

# Step 2: Delete with confirmation
pf://db::delete; users --where="status='deleted'" --confirm
# Returns: "SUCCESS: 15 row(s) deleted"
```

**Real-World**: Like checking the Recycle Bin before emptying it.

**When to Use**: Always use this workflow for important data.

---

### Use Case 5: Mass Deletion (Dangerous!)

**Scenario**: Delete all test data (use with extreme caution!)

**Command**:
```pfql
pf://db::delete; test_data --confirm
# ⚠️ DANGER: Deletes ALL rows! Requires --confirm
```

**Real-World**: Like formatting a hard drive.

**When to Use**: Only in development/test environments, never in production without backup!

---

## How to Type It

### Step-by-Step Typing Guide

**Example**: `pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'" --confirm`

1. **Type protocol**: `pf://`
2. **Type namespace**: `db::`
3. **Type command**: `delete`
4. **Add terminator**: `;` ⚠️ **CRITICAL**
5. **Add space**: ` `
6. **Type table name**: `users`
7. **Add space**: ` `
8. **Type WHERE option**: `--where=`
9. **Open quotes**: `"`
10. **Type condition**: `id='1'`
11. **Close quotes**: `"`
12. **Add space**: ` `
13. **Type confirm flag**: `--confirm`

### Common Mistakes

❌ **Missing terminator**:
```
pf://db::delete users --where="id='1'"
              ^ Missing semicolon!
```

✅ **Correct**:
```
pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'"
                ^ Semicolon here
```

❌ **No WHERE clause (dangerous!)**:
```
pf://db::delete; users
# ⚠️ DANGER: Deletes ALL users!
```

✅ **Correct** (with WHERE):
```
pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'" --confirm
# ✅ Safe: Only deletes specific user
```

❌ **Missing --confirm**:
```
pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'"
# Returns warning, doesn't delete
```

✅ **Correct**:
```
pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'" --confirm
# ✅ Proceeds with deletion
```

### Auto-Complete Hints

Most IDEs will suggest:
- After table name: `--where=` option
- After `--where=`: Column names from the table
- After condition: `--confirm` flag

---

## How to Say It

### Pronunciation Guide

**DELETE**: Pronounced "de-lete" (dee-LEET)

**Full Command Pronunciation**:
```
"P F colon slash slash D B colon colon delete semicolon users dash dash where equals quote I D equals quote one quote quote dash dash confirm"
```

**Verbal Shortcuts**:
- "Delete users where ID equals one"
- "Remove expired accounts"
- "Delete logs older than January first"

### Communication Examples

**In Code Review**:
> "We need to DELETE old log entries that are older than 30 days."

**In Documentation**:
> "Use DELETE with WHERE to remove specific rows: `pf://db::delete; table --where=\"condition\" --confirm`"

**In Team Chat**:
> "Run: `pf://db::r; test_data --where=\"status='old'\" --confirm` to clean up old test data"

**In Support**:
> "To remove that record: `pf://db::delete; users --where=\"id='123'\" --confirm`"

---

## Memory Aids

### Mnemonics

**"DELETE = Destroy Existing, Leave Empty, Erase, Terminate, Eliminate"**
- Helps remember DELETE permanently removes data

**"WHERE = Which Have Exact Requirements"**
- Helps remember WHERE specifies which rows

**"CONFIRM = Can't Override, Must Verify, Important, Required, Mandatory"**
- Helps remember --confirm is required for safety

### Visual Patterns

```
DELETE Flow:
┌─────────────┐
│ Find Rows   │ ← WHERE clause
└──────┬──────┘
       │
┌──────▼──────┐
│ Confirm?    │ ← --confirm flag
└──────┬──────┘
       │
┌──────▼──────┐
│ Remove Rows │ ← Permanent deletion
└──────┬──────┘
       │
┌──────▼──────┐
│ Return Count│
└─────────────┘
```

### Association Tricks

- **DELETE** = Like **throwing away** a document - it's gone
- **WHERE** = Like a **search filter** - find what to delete
- **CONFIRM** = Like a **safety lock** - prevents accidents
- Think of DELETE as a **permanent eraser** - use carefully!

### Quick Reference

**Pattern**: `pf://db::delete; table [--where="condition"] [--confirm]`

**Remember**:
- Always use `--where` to target specific rows
- Always use `--confirm` for safety
- ⚠️ Without WHERE, deletes ALL rows!
- ⚠️ Cannot be undone (unless you have snapshots)
- Use SELECT first to verify what will be deleted

---

## Purple Pages Integration

### Key Terms (Linked)

- **Remove** → Related to DELETE command
- **Erase** → What DELETE does
- **WHERE** → Filter clause in DELETE
- **Confirm** → Safety flag in DELETE
- **Row Deletion** → What DELETE does
- **Data Removal** → Category for DELETE
- **Permanent Deletion** → DELETE is irreversible

### Related Commands

- `SELECT` - Query rows before deleting
- `UPDATE` - Modify rows (alternative to DELETE)
- `TRUNCATE` - Remove all rows (faster than DELETE)
- `SNAPSHOT` - Create backup before deleting
- `WHERE` - Filter clause used by DELETE

### Cross-References

- See: [PFQL WHERE Command](./PFQL_Command_WHERE.md)
- See: [PFQL UPDATE Command](./PFQL_Command_UPDATE.md)
- See: [PFQL SELECT Command](./PFQL_Command_SELECT.md)
- See: [PFQL SNAPSHOT Command](./PFQL_Command_SNAPSHOT.md)
- See: [PFQL Operators Reference](../PFQL_Operators.md)

### Search Keywords

- `delete command`
- `remove rows`
- `data deletion`
- `row removal`
- `permanent delete`
- `data cleanup`
- `remove records`

---

## Developer Notes

### Implementation Details

**Location**:
- Header: `include/pfql/commands/PFQL_Command_DELETE.hpp`
- Implementation: `src/pfql/commands/PFQL_Command_DELETE.cpp`

**Algorithm**:
1. Parse command to extract table name
2. Parse WHERE clause (if present)
3. Check for confirmation flag
4. Count matching rows
5. Remove matching rows from table
6. Return count of deleted rows

**Performance Considerations**:
- DELETE is O(n) where n = number of rows
- WHERE clause evaluation adds overhead
- Iterating backwards prevents index issues
- Consider using indexes for WHERE clauses (future enhancement)

### Edge Cases

1. **No WHERE clause**: Deletes ALL rows (requires --confirm)
2. **No matching rows**: Returns "0 rows deleted"
3. **Invalid WHERE clause**: Returns error
4. **Missing --confirm**: Returns warning message
5. **Empty table**: Returns "0 rows deleted"

### Error Handling

**Common Errors**:
- `ERROR: Table is empty or invalid` - Table doesn't exist
- `ERROR: Invalid WHERE clause` - WHERE syntax error
- `ERROR: DELETE without WHERE clause requires --confirm flag` - Safety check

**Error Recovery**:
- Check table exists with SHOW TABLES
- Verify WHERE clause syntax
- Use SELECT to preview what will be deleted
- Create snapshot before deleting important data

### Safety Features

1. **--confirm flag**: Required to proceed
2. **WHERE clause warning**: Alerts when no WHERE
3. **Row count return**: Shows how many rows deleted
4. **Confirmation message**: Shows what will be deleted
5. **Cannot be undone**: Encourages careful use

---

## Examples

### Basic Examples

**Example 1: Delete Single Record**
```pfql
pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'" --confirm
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: 1 row(s) deleted`

**Example 2: Delete by Condition**
```pfql
pf://db::delete; logs --where="date < '2024-01-01'" --confirm
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: 150 row(s) deleted`

**Example 3: Using Shorthand**
```pfql
pf://db::r; users --where="id='1'" --confirm
```
**Result**: Same as DELETE (r = remove)

### Advanced Examples

**Example 4: Complex WHERE Condition**
```pfql
pf://db::delete; orders --where="status='cancelled' AND created_date < '2024-01-01'" --confirm
```
**Result**: Deletes old cancelled orders

**Example 5: Safe Deletion Workflow**
```pfql
# Step 1: Preview
pf://db::select; users --where="status='deleted'"
# Review: Shows 15 users

# Step 2: Delete
pf://db::delete; users --where="status='deleted'" --confirm
# Result: "SUCCESS: 15 row(s) deleted"
```

**Example 6: Mass Deletion (Dangerous!)**
```pfql
pf://db::delete; test_data --confirm
# ⚠️ Deletes ALL rows! Only use in test environments
```

### Real-World Scenarios

**Scenario 1: Clean Up Old Logs**
```pfql
# Create backup first
pf://admin::snapshot; backup_before_cleanup

# Then delete
pf://db::delete; logs --where="date < '2024-01-01'" --confirm
```

**Scenario 2: Remove Test Data**
```pfql
pf://db::delete; test_users --where="email LIKE '%@test.com'" --confirm
```

**Scenario 3: Delete Invalid Records**
```pfql
pf://db::delete; products --where="status='corrupted' OR status='invalid'" --confirm
```

### Common Patterns

**Pattern 1: Delete by ID**
```pfql
pf://db::delete; table_name --where="id='value'" --confirm
```

**Pattern 2: Delete by Status**
```pfql
pf://db::delete; table_name --where="status='deleted'" --confirm
```

**Pattern 3: Delete by Date**
```pfql
pf://db::delete; table_name --where="date < '2024-01-01'" --confirm
```

**Pattern 4: Safe Deletion (Always)**
```pfql
# 1. Preview first
pf://db::select; table --where="condition"

# 2. Create backup
pf://admin::snapshot; backup_name

# 3. Delete with confirmation
pf://db::delete; table --where="condition" --confirm
```

---

## Quick Reference Card

```
DELETE COMMAND QUICK REFERENCE
══════════════════════════════

Syntax: pf://db::delete; table [--where="condition"] [--confirm]

Shorthand: pf://db::r; table [--where="condition"] [--confirm]

Components:
  delete/r    Command (r = remove shorthand)
  table       Target table name
  --where=    Filter condition (HIGHLY RECOMMENDED)
  --confirm   Required flag for safety

⚠️ CRITICAL WARNINGS:
  • Without --where, deletes ALL rows!
  • Always use --confirm for safety
  • Cannot be undone (create snapshot first)
  • Use SELECT to preview before deleting

Examples:
  pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'" --confirm
  pf://db::r; logs --where="date < '2024-01-01'" --confirm
  pf://db::delete; test_data --confirm  # ⚠️ Deletes ALL!
```

---

**Last Updated**: 2025-01-XX

# PFQL MIGRATE Command
## Complete Command Documentation

**Command**: `MIGRATE`  
**Type**: Schema Migration  
**Namespace**: `db` / `admin`  
**Status**: ✅ Implemented  
**Version**: 1.0.0

---

## What It Is

MIGRATE is a **schema migration command** that applies database schema changes from migration files or migrates to a specific version. Think of it like **updating software** - it applies changes systematically.

**One-Sentence Summary**:  
"MIGRATE applies schema changes from migration files or migrates the database to a specific version."

---

## What It Does

The MIGRATE command:
1. **Reads** migration files
2. **Executes** migration commands
3. **Migrates** to target versions
4. **Supports** rollback operations
5. **Supports** dry-run preview

**Core Functionality**:
- File-based migrations
- Version-based migrations
- Rollback support
- Dry-run preview

---

## Syntax Reference

### Full Syntax

```
pf://db::migrate; migration_file [--dry-run] [--rollback]
pf://db::migrate; TO version [--dry-run] [--rollback]
```

### Terminator

**CRITICAL**: Semicolon `;` must follow `migrate`:

```
pf://db::migrate; migrations/001_add_users.sql
                ^^^^^^^^
                Terminator here
```

---

## Options & Flags

### `--dry-run`

**Description**: Preview migration without applying  
**Type**: Boolean flag  
**Required**: No

**Example**:
```pfql
pf://db::migrate; migrations/001_add_users.sql --dry-run
# Returns: "DRY-RUN: Would execute 3 migration command(s) from 'migrations/001_add_users.sql'"
```

### `--rollback`

**Description**: Rollback migration  
**Type**: Boolean flag  
**Required**: No

**Example**:
```pfql
pf://db::migrate; TO 1.0.0 --rollback
# Returns: "SUCCESS: Rolled back to version '1.0.0'"
```

---

## Examples

### Example 1: Migrate from File

```pfql
pf://db::migrate; migrations/001_add_users.sql
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: Executed 3 migration command(s) from 'migrations/001_add_users.sql'`

### Example 2: Migrate to Version

```pfql
pf://db::migrate; TO 2.0.0
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: Migrated to version '2.0.0'`

### Example 3: Dry-Run Preview

```pfql
pf://db::migrate; migrations/002_add_products.sql --dry-run
```
**Result**: `DRY-RUN: Would execute 5 migration command(s) from 'migrations/002_add_products.sql'`

---

## Migration File Format

Migration files contain PFQL commands, one per line:

```
# Migration: Add users table
CREATE TABLE users (id TEXT, name TEXT, email TEXT);

# Add index
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);

# Add column
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN status TEXT DEFAULT 'active';
```

---

**Document Version**: 1.0.0  
**Last Updated**: 2025-01-XX  
**Maintained By**: PsiForceDB Development Team

## 🔧 Implementation Details

### Database Engine Integration

**Method**: `set_database_engine(PsiForceDB::Database::PsiForceEngine* engine)`

**Usage**:
```cpp
Real_PFQL_Command_Processor processor;
processor.set_database_engine(&db_engine);
```

**Purpose**: Connects processor to database engine for executing db:: commands

---

### Shorthand Command Mapping

**Supported Shorthands**:
- `f` → `find` (SELECT)
- `a` → `add` (INSERT)
- `c` → `change` (UPDATE)
- `r` → `remove` (DELETE)
- `m` → `make` (CREATE)
- `w` → `where` (WHERE clause)
- `d` → `drop` (DROP)

**Example**:
```pfql
pf://db::f; users --where="id='1'"
# Same as: pf://db::find; users --where="id='1'"
# Executes: SELECT users --where="id='1'"
```

---

### Namespace Routing

**Supported Namespaces**:
- `db::` → Database commands (fully implemented)
- `admin::` → Admin commands (stub)
- `system::` → System commands (stub)

**Routing Logic**:
```cpp
if (cmd.namespace_name == "db") {
    return process_db_command(cmd);
} else if (cmd.namespace_name == "admin") {
    return process_admin_command(cmd);
} else if (cmd.namespace_name == "system") {
    return process_system_command(cmd);
}
```

---

### Command Processing

**Supported Commands** (db:: namespace):

1. **SELECT/FIND** (`f`)
   ```pfql
   pf://db::select; users --where="id='1'" --limit=10
   pf://db::f; users --where="status='active'"
   ```

2. **INSERT/ADD** (`a`)
   ```pfql
   pf://db::insert; users VALUES ('1', 'John', 'john@example.com')
   pf://db::a; users VALUES ('2', 'Jane', 'jane@example.com')
   ```

3. **UPDATE/CHANGE** (`c`)
   ```pfql
   pf://db::update; users SET name='Jane' --where="id='1'"
   pf://db::c; users SET email='new@example.com' --where="id='1'"
   ```

4. **DELETE/REMOVE** (`r`)
   ```pfql
   pf://db::delete; users --where="id='1'" --confirm
   pf://db::r; users --where="status='deleted'" --confirm
   ```

5. **CREATE/MAKE** (`m`)
   ```pfql
   pf://db::create; users (id TEXT, name TEXT, email TEXT)
   pf://db::m; products (id TEXT, name TEXT, price REAL)
   ```

6. **DROP** (`d`)
   ```pfql
   pf://db::drop; users
   pf://db::d; products
   ```

---

## 📊 Command Flow

```
User Input: pf://db::select; users --where="id='1'"
    ↓
PFQL_Command_Parser::parse()
    ↓
Parsed_Command {
    protocol: "pf://"
    namespace_name: "db"
    command_name: "select"
    arguments: ["users"]
    options: {"where": "id='1'"}
}
    ↓
process_pf_command()
    ↓
process_db_command() (namespace == "db")
    ↓
Build command string: "SELECT users --where=\"id='1'\""
    ↓
db_engine_->execute(command_string)
    ↓
Return PFQL_Command_Result {
    success: true
    output: "id\tname\temail\n1\tJohn\tjohn@example.com\n"
}
```

---

## ✅ Testing Checklist

- [x] Database engine reference setter
- [x] Shorthand command mapping
- [x] Namespace routing (db::)
- [x] SELECT command processing
- [x] INSERT command processing
- [x] UPDATE command processing
- [x] DELETE command processing
- [x] CREATE command processing
- [x] DROP command processing
- [x] Option parsing (--where, --limit, --confirm, --dry-run)
- [x] Error handling

---

## 🎯 Next Steps

1. ✅ Command processor integration complete
2. ⏳ Server integration (use processor in server)
3. ⏳ Codebase migration (update existing code)
4. ⏳ Admin and system namespace implementation

---

## 📝 Usage Example

```cpp
// Initialize
PsiForceDB::Database::PsiForceEngine engine("data");
Real_PFQL_Command_Processor processor;
processor.set_database_engine(&engine);

// Execute PFQL command
std::string command = "pf://db::select; users --where=\"id='1'\"";
auto result = processor.process_command(command);

if (result.success) {
    std::cout << result.output << std::endl;
} else {
    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error << std::endl;
}
```

---

**Status**: ✅ Complete  
**Integration**: ✅ Ready for server use

- Formatted output

```
pf://db::show_indexes; [ON table_name]
```

# PFQL Command Structure Map
## Visual Command Structure Reference

---

## Command Structure Diagram

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PFQL COMMAND STRUCTURE                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

[protocol]://[namespace]::[command]; [@target] [arguments] [--options]
    │           │           │          │          │           │
    │           │           │          │          │           └─ Key-value flags
    │           │           │          │          └─ Positional parameters
    │           │           │          └─ Remote target (optional)
    │           │           └─ REQUIRED TERMINATOR
    │           └─ Command category
    └─ Communication protocol

EXAMPLE:
pf://db::select; users --where="id='1'" --limit=10
│   │  │    │    │      │                │
│   │  │    │    │      │                └─ Option: limit to 10 rows
│   │  │    │    │      └─ Option: filter condition
│   │  │    │    └─ Argument: table name
│   │  │    └─ TERMINATOR (required)
│   │  └─ Command: select
│   └─ Namespace: database operations
└─ Protocol: PsiForceDB
```

---

## Protocol Routing Map

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PROTOCOL ROUTING                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

pf:// ──────► PsiForceDB Handler ──────► Database Operations
ms:// ──────► MedusaServ Handler ──────► Web Server Operations
iw:// ──────► Innocuous Access ────────► AI/Consciousness Bridge
ssh:// ─────► SSH Handler ─────────────► Remote SSH Execution
cmd:// ─────► Windows CMD Handler ────► Windows Commands
local:// ───► Local Handler ───────────► Local Script Execution

Default: pf:// (if protocol omitted)
```

---

## Namespace Hierarchy Map

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  NAMESPACE HIERARCHY                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

ROOT (Global Registry & Versioning)
│
├── CORE (Basic Primitives, Memory)
│   ├── alloc
│   ├── free
│   └── gc
│
├── ENGINE (Query Planning, Optimization)
│   ├── optimize
│   ├── plan
│   └── analyze
│
├── STORAGE (Persistence, I/O)
│   ├── backup
│   ├── restore
│   └── sync
│
├── SECURITY (Access Control, Encryption)
│   ├── encrypt
│   ├── decrypt
│   └── auth
│
├── API (External Connectors, Plugins)
│   ├── plugin_add
│   ├── api_call
│   └── script_run
│
├── DB (Database Operations) ⭐ PRIMARY
│   ├── create_table
│   ├── insert / a (shorthand)
│   ├── select / f (shorthand)
│   ├── update / c (shorthand)
│   ├── delete / r (shorthand)
│   ├── drop_table / d (shorthand)
│   ├── alter_table / m (shorthand)
│   ├── truncate / w (shorthand)
│   ├── create_index
│   ├── show_indexes
│   └── show_tables
│
├── ADMIN (Administrative Tasks)
│   ├── snapshot
│   ├── rollback
│   └── migrate
│
├── SYSTEM (System Operations)
│   ├── status
│   ├── info
│   ├── health
│   └── backup
│
└── TEMPORAL (Bitemporal Operations)
    ├── insert
    ├── query
    └── checkpoint
```

---

## Command Flow Diagram

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    COMMAND PROCESSING FLOW                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

User Input
    │
    ▼
[Parse Command String]
    │
    ├─► Extract Protocol (default: pf://)
    ├─► Extract Namespace (optional)
    ├─► Extract Command (required)
    ├─► Validate Terminator (;) ⚠️ REQUIRED
    ├─► Extract Target (@hostname)
    ├─► Extract Arguments (positional)
    └─► Extract Options (--key=value)
    │
    ▼
[Route to Handler]
    │
    ├─► pf:// ──────► process_pf_command()
    ├─► ms:// ──────► process_ms_command()
    ├─► iw:// ──────► process_iw_command()
    ├─► ssh:// ─────► process_ssh_command()
    ├─► cmd:// ─────► process_cmd_command()
    └─► local:// ───► process_local_command()
    │
    ▼
[Execute Command]
    │
    ├─► Database Operations ──► PsiForceEngine
    ├─► System Operations ────► System Handler
    ├─► Security Operations ─► Security Handler
    └─► Admin Operations ────► Admin Handler
    │
    ▼
[Return Result]
    │
    └─► Success: Output + Metadata
    └─► Error: Error Message + Suggestions
```

---

## Database Command Matrix

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              DATABASE COMMAND MATRIX                                │
├──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬───────────────────────┤
│ Operation    │ Full Command │ Shorthand    │ SQL Equivalent        │
├──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
│ Create Table │ create_table │ (none)       │ CREATE TABLE          │
│ Insert Row   │ insert       │ a (add)      │ INSERT INTO           │
│ Select Data  │ select       │ f (find)     │ SELECT                │
│ Update Row   │ update       │ c (change)   │ UPDATE                │
│ Delete Row   │ delete       │ r (remove)   │ DELETE                │
│ Alter Table  │ alter_table  │ m (modify)   │ ALTER TABLE           │
│ Truncate     │ truncate     │ w (wipe)     │ TRUNCATE              │
│ Drop Table   │ drop_table   │ d (destroy)  │ DROP TABLE            │
│ Show Tables  │ show_tables  │ (none)       │ SHOW TABLES            │
│ Create Index │ create_index │ (none)       │ CREATE INDEX           │
│ Show Indexes │ show_indexes │ (none)       │ SHOW INDEXES           │
└──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴───────────────────────┘
```

---

## WHERE Clause Operator Map

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              WHERE CLAUSE OPERATORS                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Comparison Operators:
  =   Equal to
  !=  Not equal to
  <>  Not equal to (alternative)
  >   Greater than
  <   Less than
  >=  Greater than or equal
  <=  Less than or equal

Logical Operators:
  AND  Logical AND
  OR   Logical OR
  NOT  Logical NOT (planned)

Examples:
  --where="id='1'"
  --where="age > 18"
  --where="status='active' AND age >= 21"
  --where="name='John' OR name='Jane'"
  --where="price > 100 AND category='Electronics'"
```

---

## Option Flag Reference

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  OPTION FLAG REFERENCE                      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Filtering & Querying:
  --where="condition"     Filter rows by condition
  --limit=N              Maximum number of rows to return
  --order-by=column       Sort by column name
  --format=json           Output format (json/text)

Safety & Preview:
  --dry-run              Preview changes without applying
  --confirm              Require confirmation before execution
  --preview              Show changes before applying
  --force                Force operation (skip safety checks)

Table Operations:
  --if-not-exists        Only create if doesn't exist
  --preserve-schema      Keep structure when truncating
  --after=column         Position for new column
  --default='value'      Default value for column

Data Operations:
  --batch                Enable batch mode
  --compress             Compress output/data
  --encrypt              Encrypt data
  --output=path          Output file path

System Operations:
  --detailed             Show detailed information
  --component=name       Specific component to check
  --check=type           Type of check to perform
  --full                 Full operation (vs incremental)
```

---

## Remote Target Syntax

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  REMOTE TARGET SYNTAX                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Format: @target_name

Examples:
  @10.0.0.2              IP address
  @server1               Hostname
  @192.168.1.100         IPv4 address
  @[2001:db8::1]         IPv6 address (brackets required)

Usage:
  pf://db::select; users @10.0.0.2
  pf://system::backup; @server1 --full
  ssh://system::exec; ls -la @remote_server
```

---

## Terminator Rules

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  TERMINATOR RULES                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CRITICAL: Semicolon (;) is REQUIRED after command name

✅ CORRECT:
  pf://db::select; users
  pf://system::status;
  pf://admin::snapshot; backup_2025

❌ INCORRECT:
  pf://db::select users          (missing ;)
  pf://system::status            (missing ;)
  pf://admin::snapshot backup    (missing ;)

Position:
  [protocol]://[namespace]::[command]; [rest...]
                                    ↑
                              REQUIRED HERE

Error Message:
  ERROR: Missing terminator ';' after command_name
  Suggestion: Did you mean: pf://db::select; users?
```

---

## Command Examples by Category

### Database Operations
```
CREATE:  pf://db::create_table; users (id, name, email)
INSERT:  pf://db::insert; users '1' 'John' 'john@example.com'
SELECT:  pf://db::select; users --where="id='1'"
UPDATE:  pf://db::update; users set name='Jane' --where="id='1'"
```

### Security Operations

## Quick Command Builder

# PFQL TRUNCATE Command
## Complete Command Documentation

**Command**: `TRUNCATE`  
**Type**: Data Removal  
**Namespace**: `db`  
**Status**: ✅ Implemented  
**Version**: 1.0.0

---

## What It Is

TRUNCATE is a **data removal command** that quickly removes all rows from a table while preserving the table structure. Think of it like **emptying a filing cabinet** - all files are gone, but the cabinet structure remains.

**One-Sentence Summary**:  
"TRUNCATE removes all rows from a table while keeping the table structure intact."

---

## What It Does

The TRUNCATE command:
1. **Removes** all rows from a table
2. **Preserves** table structure (columns remain)
3. **Requires** confirmation for safety
4. **Returns** count of deleted rows
5. **Faster** than DELETE (no row-by-row processing)

**Core Functionality**:
- Clear all table data
- Keep table structure
- Safety confirmation
- Fast operation

---

## Syntax Reference

### Full Syntax

```
pf://db::truncate; table_name [--confirm]
```

### Terminator

**CRITICAL**: Semicolon `;` must follow `truncate`:

```
pf://db::truncate; users --confirm
                ^^^^^^^^
                Terminator here
```

---

## Options & Flags

### `--confirm`

**Description**: Confirmation flag for truncation  
**Type**: Boolean flag  
**Required**: Yes  
**Default**: false

**⚠️ WARNING**: TRUNCATE requires `--confirm` to proceed!

**Example**:
```pfql
pf://db::truncate; users --confirm
# Proceeds with truncation

pf://db::truncate; users
# Returns: "⚠️ WARNING: This will delete all N row(s)... Add --confirm to proceed"
```

---

## Use Cases

### Use Case 1: Clear Test Data

**Scenario**: Remove all test data from a table

**Command**:
```pfql
pf://db::truncate; test_users --confirm
```

**Real-World**: Like clearing a test database before running new tests.

---

### Use Case 2: Reset Table

**Scenario**: Reset a table to empty state

**Command**:
```pfql
pf://db::truncate; logs --confirm
```

**Real-World**: Like clearing a log file while keeping the file structure.

---

## Examples

### Example 1: Truncate Table

```pfql
pf://db::truncate; users --confirm
```
**Result**: `SUCCESS: 150 row(s) truncated from table 'users'`

### Example 2: Without Confirmation

```pfql
pf://db::truncate; users
```
**Result**: `⚠️ WARNING: This will delete all 150 row(s) from table 'users'... Add --confirm to proceed`

---

## TRUNCATE vs DELETE

| Feature | TRUNCATE | DELETE |
|---------|----------|--------|
| Speed | Fast (bulk operation) | Slower (row-by-row) |
| WHERE clause | No (all rows) | Yes (selective) |
| Table structure | Preserved | Preserved |
| Confirmation | Required | Required |
| Use case | Clear all data | Remove specific rows |

---

**Document Version**: 1.0.0  
**Last Updated**: 2025-01-XX  
**Maintained By**: PsiForceDB Development Team
